title: Access modifiers (visibility and encapsulation)
hook: Access modifiers control who can see your types and members. The Common Language Runtime (CLR) enforces them at run time — unlike TypeScript `private`, which disappears after compilation.

blocks.text: Every type and member has an **accessibility level** that determines which code can reference it. C# has seven modifiers you should be able to name in an interview: `public`, `private`, `protected`, `internal`, `protected internal`, `private protected`, and `file`. Members default to `private`; top-level types default to `internal`.

entries.plainDefinition: Visible to any code in any assembly.
entries.example: `public class ApiClient` — any project can reference it.

entries.plainDefinition: Visible only inside the containing type. Default for members.
entries.example: `private readonly byte[] _key;` — only methods in the same class can access it.

entries.plainDefinition: Visible within the same assembly (project output). Default for top-level types.
entries.example: `internal class TokenParser` — hidden from other projects.

entries.plainDefinition: A top-level type visible only in the declaring source file. Used by source generators.
entries.example: `file static class ParserHelpers` — invisible outside this .cs file.

blocks.text: Encapsulation is a CLR contract, not a comment. Your public surface is a compatibility promise — once something is public, removing or changing it breaks callers. `internal` is for your application's own composition. `private` is where signing keys and parsing logic should live. In interviews, know the difference between `protected internal` (union: same assembly OR derived) and `private protected` (intersection: derived AND same assembly).

blocks.title: protected internal vs private protected
blocks.body: `protected internal` = visible to the assembly OR to derived types anywhere (OR). `private protected` = visible only to derived types in the same assembly (AND). This is a favorite interview trap.

items.title: private
items.body: Containing type only. Default for members.

items.title: internal
items.body: Same assembly only. Default for top-level types.

items.title: protected
items.body: Containing type plus any derived type, in any assembly.

items.title: protected internal
items.body: Same assembly OR derived types elsewhere.

items.title: private protected
items.body: Derived types that are also in the same assembly.

items.title: file
items.body: Declaring source file only. Top-level types only.

diagram.title: Access modifier visibility
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  P[public] --> ALL[Any assembly]
  I[internal] --> ASM[Same assembly]
  PR[private] --> TYPE[Containing type]
  PT[protected] --> DER[Derived types]
  PI[protected internal] --> ASM
  PI --> DER
  PP[private protected] --> ASM
  PP --> DER
  F[file] --> FILE[Same source file]

snippet.label: protected internal vs file-local helper
snippet.explanation: Line 1: `internal` hides `TokenParser` from other assemblies. Line 4: `private` field for the signing key. Line 8: `protected internal` visible to the assembly and derived types elsewhere. Line 11: `file` makes `ParserHelpers` invisible outside this source file.

snippet.label: private protected in action
snippet.explanation: Line 3: `private protected` allows access only from derived types in the same assembly. A derived class in another project gets a compile error.

snippet.label: InternalsVisibleTo for test assemblies
snippet.explanation: Line 1: `InternalsVisibleTo` opens `internal` types to a named test assembly. This is an assembly-level hole, not a language backdoor — the test project still needs the attribute.

blocks.title: Privacy in C# vs JS/TS
rows: CLR enforces `private` at runtime via metadata
TS `private` is erased; JS `#field` is runtime but not metadata
JS modules hide unexported names — closest to `internal`/`file`
No equivalent — export or use dependency injection

blocks.title: Confusing protected internal with private protected
blocks.body: `protected internal` is more permissive (OR). `private protected` is more restrictive (AND). Draw a Venn diagram in your head during interviews.

blocks.title: Shipping public DTOs meant to be internal
blocks.body: Once a type is public, every field and method on it is part of your compatibility contract. Start `internal` and promote to `public` deliberately.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: protected internal is union — visible in the assembly OR to derived types anywhere. private protected is intersection — derived AND same assembly only. Draw the Venn diagram in FAANG loops. file-local types (C# 11) keep source-generator helpers from polluting public API — they never appear in consumer IntelliSense. InternalsVisibleTo opens internal to friend assemblies — common in test projects but a security review item for auth libraries. TypeScript private erases; C# private is enforced by the CLR at run time.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Swapping protected internal and private protected definitions. Saying TypeScript private equals C# private at run time. Using public on every DTO by default. Not knowing file is for types in one file.

interviewTakeaways: Members default private; top-level types default internal.
protected internal is OR; private protected is AND.
file keeps types file-local — common with source generators.
60s: protected internal is union. private protected is intersection. file is file-scoped type. CLR enforces; TS private erases.
Follow-up: when do you use InternalsVisibleTo?
commonPitfalls: Confusing protected internal with private protected gets you rejected.
Shipping public DTOs meant to be internal.
Strong answer: 'protected internal OR. private protected AND. file for generator helpers. Start internal, promote deliberately.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: TypeScript `private` is erased at compile time. ECMAScript `#fields` are a runtime hurdle but not CLR accessibility. C# modifiers survive in metadata and are checked by the runtime.
JavaScript modules hide unbound names by not exporting them. That is file/module scope, closest to C# `internal`/`file`, not to CLR `private` on a member.
